source_text: Quamquam primo libro religiones deorum falsas esse monstrauerim, quod ii quorum uarios dissimilesque cultus per uniuersam terram consensus hominum stulta persuasione suscepit, mortales fuerint functique uita diuinae necessitati morte concesserint, tamen ne qua dubitatio relinquatur, hic secundus liber fontem ipsum patefaciet errorum causasque omnes explicabit, quibus decepti homines et primitus deos esse crediderint et postmodum persuasione inueterata in susceptis prauissime religionibus perseuerauerint. gestio enim conuictis inanus et hominum inpia uanitate detecta singularis dei adserere maiestatem, suscipiens utilius et maius officium reuocandi homines a prauis itineribus et in gratiam secum ipsos reducendi, ne se, ut quidam philosophi faciunt, tanto opere despiciant neue se infirmos et superuacuos et nihili et frustra omnino natos putent, quae opinio plerosque ad uitia compellit. nani dum existimant nulli deo esse nos curae aut post mortem nihil futuros, totos se libidinibus addicunt et dum licere sibi putant, hauriendis uoluptatibus sitienter incumbunt, per quas inprudentes in laqueos mortis incurrant. ignorant enim quae sit hominis ratio: quam si tenere uellent, in primis dominum suum agnoscerent, uirtutem iustitiamque sequerentur, terrenis figmentis animas suas non substernerent, mortiferas libidinum suauitates non adpeterent, denique se ipsos magni aestimarent atque intellegerent plus esse in homine quam uidetur: cuius uim condicionemque non aliter posse retineri, nisi cultum ueri parentis sui deposita prauitate susceperint. equidem sicut oportet de summa rerum saepenumero cogitans admirari soleo, maiestatem dei singularis quae continet regitque omnia in tantam uenisse obliuionem, ut quae sola debeat coli, sola potissimum neclegatur, homines autem ipsos ad tantam caecitatem esse deductos, ut uero ac uiuo deo mortuos praeferant, terrenos autem sepultosque in terra ei qui fundator ipsius terrae fuit. et tamen huic inpietati hominum posset uenia concedi, si omnino ab ignorantia diuini nominis ueniret hic error. cum uero ipsos deorum cultores saepe uideamus deum summum et confiteri et praedicare, quam sibi ueniam sperare possint inpietatis suae qui non adgnoscunt cultum eius, quem prorsus ignorari ab homine fas non est? nam et cum iurant et cum optant et cum gratias agunt, non Iouem aut deos multos, sed deum nominant: adeo ueritas ipsa cogente natura etiam ab inuitis pectoribus erumpit. quod quidem non faciunt in prosperis rebus. nam tum maxime deus ex memoria hominum elabitur, cum beneficiis eius fruentes honorem dare diuinae indulgentiae debent. at uero si qua necessitas grauis presserit, tunc deum recordantur: si belli terror infremuit, si morborum pestifera uis incubuit, si alimenta frugibus longa siccitas denegauit, si saeua tempestas, si grando ingruit., ad deum confugitur, a deo petitur auxilium, deus ut subueniat oratur. si quis in mari uento saeuiente iactatur, hunc inuocat, si quis aliqua ui adflictatur, hunc potius inplorat, si quis ad extremam mendicandi necessitatem deductus uictum precibus exposcit, deum solum obtestatur, per eius diuinum atque unicum nomen hominum sibi misericordiam quaerit. numquam igitur dei meminerunt, nisi dum in malis sunt: postquam metus deseruit et pericula recesserunt, tum uero alacres ad deorum templa concurrunt, his libant, his sacrificant, hos coronant. deo autem quem in ipsa necessitate implorauerant, ne uerbo quidem gratias agunt. adeo ex rerum prosperitate luxuria, ex luxuria uero ut uitia omnia sic inpietas aduersus deum nascitur. quanam istut ex causa fieri putemus nisi esse aliquam peruersam potestatem, quae ueritati sit semper inimica, quae humanis erroribus gaudeat, cui unum ac perpetuum sit opus offundere tenebras et hominum caecare mentes, ne lucem uideant, ne denique in caelum aspiciant ac naturam corporis sui seruent? nam cum ceterae animantes pronis corporibus in humum spectent, quia rationem ac sapientiam non acceperunt, nobis autem status rectus, sublimis uultus ab artifice deo datus sit, apparet istas religiones deorum non esse rationis humanae, quia curuant caeleste animal ad ueneranda terrena. parens enim noster ille unus et solus cum fingeret hominem id est animal intellegens et rationis capax, eum uero ex humo subleuatum ad contemplationem sui artificis erexit. quod optime ingeniosus poeta signauit: pronaque cum spectent animalia cetera terram, os homini sublime dedit caelumque uidere iussit et erectos ad sidera tollere uultus. hinc utique ἄνθρωπον Graeci appellauerunt, quod sursum spectet. ipsi ergo sibi renuntiant seque hominum nomine abdicant qui non sursum aspiciunt, sed deorsum: nisi forte id ipsum quod recti sumus sine causa homini adtributum putant. spectare nos caelum deus uoluit utique non frustra. nam et aues et ex mutis paene omnia caelum uident, sed nobis proprie datum est caelum rigidis ac stantibus intueri, ut religionem ibi quaeramus, ut deum, cuius illa sedes est, quoniam oculis non possumus, animo contemplemur: quod profecto non facit qui aes aut lapidem, quae sunt terrena, ueneratur. est autem prauissimum, cum ratio corporis recta sit, quod est temporale, ipsum uero animum, qui sit aeternus, humilem fieri, cum figura et status nihil aliut significet nisi mentem hominis eo spectare oportere quo uultum, et animum tam rectum esse debere quam corpus, ut id cui dominari debet imitetur. uerum homines et nominis sui et rationis obliti oculos suos ab alto deiciunt soloque defigunt ac timent opera digitorum suorum, quasi uero quicquam esse possit artifice suo maius.
pass_a_gloss: Book 2 opens fontem errorum after Book 1 showed mortal 'gods'. Goal: assert singularis dei maiestas; recall from praua itinera; know ueri parentis cultum. Even pagans cry 'deus' in crisis then return to temples. Perverse power blinds. Upright human status for caelum/religio—not venerating aes/lapidem digitorum.
pass_b_english: Although in the first book I showed that the religions of the gods are false—because those whose varied and unlike cults the consensus of humans across the whole earth took up by foolish persuasion were mortals and, having finished life, yielded to divine necessity by death—nevertheless, lest any doubt remain, this second book will lay open the very font of errors and explain all the causes by which deceived humans both at first believed there are gods and afterward, by persuasion grown old, persisted in religions most crookedly taken up.

For I am eager, with empty things convicted and humans' impious vanity detected, to assert the majesty of the singular God, taking up the more useful and greater office of recalling humans from crooked paths and bringing them back into favor with themselves, lest—as some philosophers do—they despise themselves so greatly and think themselves weak and superfluous and of no account and born wholly in vain, which opinion drives many to vices. For while they think we are no god's care or will be nothing after death, they give themselves wholly to lusts and, while they think it is allowed them, eagerly press upon draining pleasures, through which unwise they run into death's snares.

For they do not know what the reason of the human is: which if they wished to hold, they would first recognize their Lord, follow virtue and justice, not lay their souls under earthly figments, not seek the death-bearing sweets of lusts, finally value themselves highly and understand there is more in the human than appears—whose force and condition cannot otherwise be kept unless, having put down crookedness, they take up the cult of their true Parent.

Indeed, as often as I think as one ought about the summit of things, I am accustomed to wonder that the majesty of the singular God which contains and rules all things has come into such forgetfulness that what alone ought to be worshiped is above all neglected, and that humans themselves have been led to such blindness that they prefer the dead to the true and living God, and those earthly and buried in earth to Him who was Founder of the earth itself. And yet pardon could be granted this impiety of humans if this error came wholly from ignorance of the divine name. But when we often see the very worshipers of the gods both confess and proclaim the highest God, what pardon of their impiety can they hope for who do not recognize the cult of Him whom it is not right for a human to be wholly ignorant of?

For both when they swear and when they wish and when they give thanks, they name not Jupiter or many gods but God: so much does truth itself, with nature compelling, burst even from unwilling breasts. Which indeed they do not do in prosperous affairs. For then especially God slips from humans' memory when, enjoying His benefits, they ought to give honor to divine kindness. But if some heavy necessity has pressed, then they remember God: if war's terror has roared, if disease's pestilent force has settled, if long drought has denied food to crops, if a savage storm, if hail rushes in—to God there is fleeing, from God help is sought, God is prayed to come to aid.

If anyone is tossed on the sea with raging wind, he calls on this One; if anyone is struck by some force, he rather implores this One; if anyone, reduced to the extreme need of begging, seeks food by prayers, he adjures God alone and through His divine and unique name seeks humans' mercy for himself. Therefore they never remember God except while they are in evils: after fear has left and dangers have withdrawn, then eagerly they run together to the gods' temples, pour to these, sacrifice to these, crown these. But to God whom they had implored in the very necessity they do not give thanks even by a word. So much from prosperity of things is born luxury, and from luxury, as all vices, so also impiety against God.

For what cause should we think this happens except that there is some perverse power which is always enemy to truth, which rejoices in human errors, whose one and perpetual work is to pour darkness and blind humans' minds lest they see the light, lest finally they look into heaven and keep the nature of their own body? For since the other living things with prone bodies look to the ground because they did not receive reason and wisdom, but to us a straight stance and uplifted face was given by God the craftsman, it appears that those religions of the gods are not of human reason, because they bend the heavenly animal to venerating earthly things.

For that one and only Parent of ours, when He fashioned the human—that is, an intelligent animal capable of reason—raised him, lifted from the soil, to contemplation of his Craftsman. Which the ingenious poet marked best: and while other animals look prone at the earth, He gave the human a lofty face and ordered him to see heaven and lift upright faces to the stars. Hence of course the Greeks called him anthropos, because he looks upward. Therefore they renounce themselves and abdicate the name of humans who do not look upward but downward—unless perhaps they think that very thing, that we are upright, was assigned to the human without cause. God wished us to look at heaven, and not in vain. For birds too and almost all from the mute see heaven, but to us it was properly given to gaze at heaven rigid and standing, that we might seek religion there, that we might contemplate with the mind God whose seat that is, since we cannot with eyes—which indeed one who venerates bronze or stone, which are earthly, does not do.

And it is most crooked that, when the body's reason is upright—which is temporal—the mind itself, which is eternal, should be made low, when figure and stance signify nothing other than that the human mind ought to look where the face does, and that the mind ought to be as upright as the body, so that it may imitate that which it ought to rule. But humans, forgetful of their name and reason, cast their eyes down from on high and fix them on the ground and fear the works of their own fingers, as if anything could be greater than its craftsman.
